extracted.subtask_description: Techniques and typical solution patterns for contest-style problems using the Extremal Principle and the Box (pigeonhole) Principle, with worked examples and problem templates. Focused on identifying extreme elements, constructing pigeonhole partitions, and common auxiliary maneuvers (projections, parity classes, modulo sums, ordering by angle, etc.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Extremal Principle — choose an extreme element
rubrics_metrics.description: Choose an element with an extreme property (minimum or maximum) and use its extremality to derive structural information or a contradiction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used throughout the chapter: e.g., choose the smallest distance among intersection points and derive contradictions (solution 2); pick the largest pile in a chip-splitting game to decide winning strategy (solution 4); choose the point joined to the maximum number m of other points to partition the graph and bound edges (solution 11); choose the smallest square in a cube dissection to force a contradiction (solution 17). Typical pattern: assume contrary, pick an extremal object, show that any alternative violates extremality, produce contradiction or desired property.

rubrics_metrics.name: Box Principle (Pigeonhole Principle) — basic formulation
rubrics_metrics.description: If (n+1) pearls are put into n boxes, then at least one box has more than one pearl.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The textbook emphasizes recognizing existence problems where the box principle applies. It gives many standard applications (E1–E11): equal acquaintance counts (E1), runs of games (E2), subset-sum divisible by n via partial sums (E3), two numbers one divisible by the other among n+1 numbers from {1,..,2n} (E4), existence of multiplicative inverses mod b (E5), Erdős–Szekeres monotone subsequence bounds (E6), lattice midpoint via parity classes (E7), periodicity of mod-10 Fibonacci-like sequences (E8), bounding periods and forcing a zero term mod 10^n (E9), powers ending with ...0001 (E10), overlapping rugs area bound (E11).

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical advice for applying pigeonhole: identify pearls and boxes
rubrics_metrics.description: The main difficulty when applying the Box Principle is identifying what to treat as 'pearls' and what as 'boxes'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text explicitly remarks that the principle 'gives no help in finding a multiply occupied box' and that identifying pearls/boxes is the central modeling step. Examples show common choices: persons → boxes labeled by number of acquaintances (E1), partial sums → boxes labeled by residues mod n (E3), pairs of consecutive terms → boxes labeled by ordered pairs when studying periodicity (E8). Also sometimes constraints reduce possible boxes (e.g., in E1 boxes 0 and n−1 cannot both be occupied).

rubrics_metrics.name: Partial-sums mod n trick to find divisible subset
rubrics_metrics.description: Consider the sequence of prefix sums s1, s2, ..., sn modulo n; if any si ≡ 0 mod n take that prefix, otherwise two si share the same remainder and their difference is a subsequence sum divisible by n.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explicitly given in E3. This is a standard pigeonhole application for integer sequences to produce a nonempty subset with sum divisible by n. Variants appear in proofs about Fibonacci modulo periods and related divisibility arguments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bounding periodicity by considering ordered pairs of consecutive terms
rubrics_metrics.description: Model a (linear) recurrence modulo M by ordered pairs (a_k, a_{k+1}); since there are at most M^2 possible pairs, by pigeonhole some pair repeats and the sequence becomes periodic.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used in E8 and E9 to bound periods of mod-10 and mod-10^n Fibonacci-like sequences and to deduce that a zero term occurs in the period. The text notes the pair (0,0) may be impossible, reducing the upper bound on distinct pairs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Projection to a line to detect common intersection
rubrics_metrics.description: Project polygons or geometric objects onto a line and reduce a multi-dimensional intersection problem to overlapping intervals on that line; then use endpoints/ordering to find a common projected point whose perpendicular gives the intersection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Stated in solution to problem 20: project all polygons onto a line g, obtain segments with a common intersection point; choose the rightmost left-endpoint to guarantee a point belonging to all projections, and lift it perpendicularly to get the intersection in the plane.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choose longest chord/diameter to characterize bodies (maximal chord method)
rubrics_metrics.description: Select a longest chord (pair of farthest points) of a solid/planar set and analyze cross-sections through it (circles with that diameter) to deduce the set is a ball/disk.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applied in problems 9 and 10: pick two points at maximum distance, draw the circle with that diameter and show every interior point lies inside the circle by geometric/continuity arguments. The text notes one must assume the solid is closed and bounded and may invoke Weierstrass theorem to guarantee maxima; elementary alternatives exist but are longer.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ordering by angle / median selection to balance inside/outside counts
rubrics_metrics.description: When given points on one side of a line or circle, order them by an angular measure and choose the median index to get exactly balanced counts inside vs outside a constructed circle.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used in problem 24: For 2n+3 points with no three collinear and no four cocircular, order points X1,...,X2n+1 by angle AXiB and take X_{n+1}; the circle through A,X_{n+1},B contains exactly n of the other 2n points. This is a general selection-by-ordering technique to achieve balanced partitions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Parity / coordinate classifying to force lattice midpoints
rubrics_metrics.description: Classify lattice points by parity pattern of coordinates (even/odd). Two points with identical parity pattern have a midpoint which is a lattice point.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Given as E7: with five lattice points there are only four parity classes, so two must share a class; their midpoint is integral because sums of coordinates are even. This is a standard combinatorial geometry pigeonhole application.

rubrics_metrics.name: Counting and double-counting to bound quantities in graphs/social networks
rubrics_metrics.description: Count pairs or edges in two ways and combine inequalities to bound numbers of special vertices (e.g., students who are 'better than majority of their friends') or to force existence of vertices with certain degrees.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applied in problems 37, 38, 42, 44: e.g., bound number x of 'good' students by counting ordered pairs where a student is the better in a friend pair; select person with maximal acquaintances and use degree arguments to deduce existence of a person with exactly one friend (38); compare sums and use ordering to deduce inequalities for permutations of reciprocals (42). The typical recipe: identify pairs to count, lower/upper bound that count in two ways, solve resulting inequality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of extremal angles/triangle inequalities to bound distances and areas
rubrics_metrics.description: Use maximal/minimal angle considerations and basic trigonometric/triangle inequalities to obtain bounds on side lengths, ratios, or areas (e.g., to force two points to be close or bound area by product of heights).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used in problems 16, 23, 28: e.g., among six points there is a triangle with an angle ≥ 120°, which yields side-ratio bounds; in problem 23 use hb≤|BB1|≤1 and hc≤|CC1|≤1 and sine monotonicity to bound triangle area ≤ 1/√3; in 28 use pigeonhole on central angles among 8 points to force an arc <60° and thus chord length <1. These are routine geometric extremal/inequality patterns.
